specification.problem: Approximate a single-qubit z-rotation R_z(\theta) to precision \varepsilon by a Pauli+V circuit (gates V_1,V_2,V_3, their inverses, and Paulis) of small V-count, adapting the Ross–Selinger deterministic-search technique (lattice-point enumeration in an \varepsilon-region followed by a number-theoretic solvability test) from the Clifford+T / \mathbb{Z}[\omega] setting to the Pauli+V / \mathbb{Z}[i] setting.
specification.reconstruction_scope: One instance of the synthesis problem: a single target rotation R_z(\theta) with \theta=\pi/4 and \varepsilon=0.1 (both chosen here as an assumption, since the abstract gives no instance). The scope covers (i) the algebraic form of Pauli+V unitaries, (ii) the \varepsilon-region criterion, (iii) the search over Gaussian integers a in the scaled region and the two-squares test yielding b, and (iv) delegation of the final gate word to a Pauli+V exact-synthesis routine. Outside scope: the paper's specific geometric lemmas and constants, any proven V-count bound (e.g. as a function of \log(1/\varepsilon)), running-time analysis, the precise enumeration order/grid traversal of the deterministic search, and the exact-synthesis algorithm's internal details.

symbols.meaning: The three V gates (Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak / Harrow–Recht–Chuang generators)
Denominator exponent of \sqrt{5}; equals the V-count of the synthesized circuit under the exact-synthesis normalization
Gaussian-integer entries of the scaled unitary 5^{k/2}U
\varepsilon-region in the unit disk around e^{-i\theta/2}
Residual norm n=5^k-|a|^2 that must be a sum of two integer squares

equations.label: V gates
equations.description: Definition of the V gates generating, together with the Pauli group, the Pauli+V gate set; V-count counts occurrences of V_j^{\pm1}.
equations.justification: Standard definition of the V basis used in Pauli+V synthesis literature (Harrow–Recht–Chuang; Bocharov–Gurevich–Svore); the abstract only names the framework.

equations.label: Target z-rotation
equations.description: The single-qubit z-rotation to be approximated.
equations.justification: Standard convention for z-rotations; the abstract states the problem is approximating z-rotations.
assumptions: Convention with half-angle; other conventions rescale \theta.

equations.label: Form of Pauli+V unitaries
equations.latex: U=5^{-k/2}\begin{pmatrix} a & -\bar b\\ b & \bar a\end{pmatrix},\quad a,b\in\mathbb{Z}[i],\quad |a|^2+|b|^2=5^k
equations.description: Up to global phase, every Pauli+V circuit of V-count k yields a unitary of this form; conversely such a matrix with k minimal (5^{k/2}U not further divisible so as to lower k) is exactly synthesizable with V-count k.
equations.justification: Each V_j equals (1/\sqrt5) times a matrix over \mathbb{Z}[i], so products of k V's have this form; the converse (exact synthesis with V-count equal to the minimal denominator exponent) is the Bocharov–Gurevich–Svore exact-synthesis result, recalled from background, not from the abstract.
assumptions: Pauli factors and global phases are absorbed; the precise divisibility/normal-form condition for minimality of k is not restated here.

equations.label: \varepsilon-region criterion
equations.description: For U of the form in eq_3, operator-norm closeness to R_z(\theta) depends only on the normalized entry u lying in the thin circular-segment region R_\varepsilon.
equations.justification: This is the \varepsilon-region reduction used by Ross–Selinger for unitaries of the form [[u,-\bar t],[t,\bar u]]; it is independent of the gate set and so carries over to Pauli+V. Recalled as background, not extracted from the paper.
assumptions: Distance measured in operator norm with U fixed up to global phase; a different metric changes the constant 1-\varepsilon^2/2.

equations.label: Lattice search condition (deterministic search)
equations.latex: a\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\cap 5^{k/2}R_\varepsilon,\qquad\text{enumerated for } k=0,1,2,\dots \text{ until a solution of eq\_6 is found}
equations.description: Candidate entries a are the Gaussian-integer lattice points inside the scaled \varepsilon-region (area \approx 5^k\cdot\mathrm{area}(R_\varepsilon)); the search is deterministic: enumerate all lattice points for the current k before incrementing k.
equations.abstract_quote: We adapt the deterministic-search technique to the case of Pauli+V circuits and prove similar results. Because of the relative simplicity of the Pauli+V framework, we use much simpler geometric methods.
equations.justification: Inference: Ross–Selinger's deterministic search enumerates ring elements in an \varepsilon-region; in Pauli+V the relevant ring is \mathbb{Z}[i], a planar lattice, so the 'simpler geometric methods' plausibly refer to counting/enumerating lattice points of \mathbb{Z}[i] in a planar region rather than the four-dimensional \mathbb{Z}[\omega] embedding. The exact enumeration order and any grid transformation used in the paper are not given by the abstract.
assumptions: The paper's search region is (a scaling of) R_\varepsilon or a simply shaped subset of it; the precise shape and traversal are unknown.

equations.label: Two-squares solvability for b
equations.description: Given a candidate a, the second entry b exists iff the residual n is a sum of two squares; b is then computed by factoring n (or Cornacchia's algorithm). This replaces Ross–Selinger's Diophantine step over \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2].
equations.justification: Fermat's two-squares theorem (norms from \mathbb{Z}[i]); the role of this step in the Pauli+V adaptation is inferred from eq_3's unitarity constraint.
assumptions: Factorization of n (size about 5^k) is feasible for the tiny instance; the paper may instead use a probabilistic or restricted test (e.g. n prime), which the abstract does not specify.

registers.name: q
registers.role: Single data qubit on which the synthesized Pauli+V approximation of R_z(\theta) acts

specification.initial_state: Not fixed by the problem: the output is a gate sequence U\approx R_z(\theta) to be applied to an arbitrary single-qubit state |\psi\rangle.

steps.description: Fix the target \theta and precision \varepsilon (toy instance: \theta=\pi/4, \varepsilon=0.1); form the \varepsilon-region R_\varepsilon around e^{-i\theta/2}.
For the current denominator exponent k (starting at k=0), deterministically enumerate all Gaussian integers a in the scaled region 5^{k/2}R_\varepsilon.
For each candidate a, compute n=5^k-|a|^2 and test whether n is a sum of two squares; if so, compute b with |b|^2=n and stop. If no candidate succeeds, increment k and return to the previous step.
Assemble the exactly representable unitary U=5^{-k/2}[[a,-\bar b],[b,\bar a]]; it satisfies \|U-R_z(\theta)\|\le\varepsilon by construction.
Run a Pauli+V exact-synthesis routine on U to obtain a word in V_1^{\pm1},V_2^{\pm1},V_3^{\pm1} and Paulis of V-count k; apply this word to the data qubit.

specification.classical_postprocessing: All search steps (lattice enumeration, two-squares test, exact synthesis into a V/Pauli word) are classical preprocessing; no quantum measurement or postprocessing is part of the method itself.
assumptions: Toy instance \theta=\pi/4, \varepsilon=0.1 chosen by the reconstructor; the abstract gives no instance.
Global phases are ignored and Pauli gates are free (not counted) in the V-count.
Operator-norm distance with the Ross–Selinger \varepsilon-region reduction is assumed to be the metric used.
The Bocharov–Gurevich–Svore exact-synthesis result (V-count equals minimal \sqrt5-denominator exponent) is assumed available as a black box.
missing_information: The paper's specific 'simpler geometric methods' (lemmas, constants, shape of the search region, lattice-point counting arguments).
Any proven bound on the resulting V-count as a function of \log(1/\varepsilon), and whether it is a worst-case or heuristic/average-case result.
The precise deterministic enumeration order and stopping criteria, and whether the two-squares step uses full factorization, a primality restriction, or another test.
Exact-synthesis normal form and divisibility conditions guaranteeing V-count exactly k for the found (a,b).
Whether the paper also treats non-z rotations or general unitaries, and any numerical results.
